visual_source_files.tool: PNG rendered asset embedded by README
visual_source_files.evidence: README title/abstract match the ICML 2026 paper and the image labels, two input paths, frozen layers, skip/recurrent modules, output, and pseudocode match PDF Figure 1; no editable figure source is present in the tree.

source_acquisition.search_note: Inventory row reports no_public_source_found and suggests tianyi-lab/PoLar. The PDF first page explicitly links that repository; gh repo metadata and README strictly match the title and ICML 2026 version. The read-only main-tree inspection found only search_space.png as a visual asset and no plot/table scripts, notebooks, LaTeX/TikZ, or figure-specific data. corpus/visual_sources/icml-2026-01423817c82b/ is empty or absent. Therefore only Figure 1 is credited with a matching rendered asset; all other figures/tables remain without public direct visual source.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Baseline/original is commonly orange and Base commonly blue; budget traces use a blue sequential gradient, while model/difficulty categories use categorical colors. Tables use black/gray booktabs with blue Gain or lavender PoLAR highlights. The mapping is locally consistent but not a single global registry.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: PDF text, table rules, arrows, axes, and captions are vector; imported conceptual assets and statistical plot images contain raster components. Figure 1/2 and Figures 3–8 are mixed-rendered; Tables 1–11 are text/rule/vector objects.
paper_style.style_consistency: The Letter two-column skeleton, caption placement, Roman/math body typography, and booktabs table grammar are stable. Imported diagram assets and plot exports differ in sans-serif font, size, and color treatment, and narrow facets/wide tables trade readability for coverage.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. Program-of-layers (PoLAR) for two different inputs. The D layers in a pretrained LLM define D functions f_0, …, f_{D−1}. Instead of calling them in a static fixed order from f_0 to f_{D−1}, the dynamic inference of PoLAR executes an input-specific program π = (i_1, …, i_K) that calls the functions with layer skipping and recurrence. PoLAR enables a training-free architecture of dynamic depth for different inputs, yielding diverse latent computations that cannot be fully covered by existing methods.

color.semantic_mapping: Cyan input and orange output boxes, green recurrent modules, blue arrows, and black/white layer boxes; operation words and arrow styles reinforce role.

encodings.x: left-to-right input → frozen-layer → output execution direction
encodings.y: two input-specific program cases and the aligned pseudocode blocks
encodings.shape: rounded boxes for input, recurrent segment, output; layer rectangles and dashed skipped layer
encodings.line: solid versus dashed blue arrows and loop brackets
encodings.facet: upper x_0 path versus lower x_1 path
encodings.text: layer labels, π, operation names, ellipses, and pseudocode

figures.data_and_statistics: Mechanism diagram only. Each input is paired with an example program π=(i_1,…,i_K) over a frozen D-layer function library; there are no observations, sample counts, denominators, aggregation, repeated trials, failures, or uncertainty intervals.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduces the paper claim that a static forward pass is one member of a larger latent execution space. It provides the vocabulary used by Figure 2, motivates the MCTS observations in Figures 3–7, and frames the learned program predictor evaluated in Tables 2–11 and Figure 8.
design_strengths: Two input-specific paths show skip and recurrence with both execution arrows and pseudocode.
A shared frozen-layer library visually anchors the method before quantitative results.
The public search_space.png asset is a close content match and can be reused as a rendered conceptual source.
design_weaknesses: The schematic is not to scale, so D, d, and ellipses do not reveal a numeric program length.
Module color differences collapse in grayscale and the pseudocode becomes small at single-column size.
The caption does not state the segment-length bound or how the predictor is trained.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use two input-specific paths through the same frozen function library, pairing colored operation blocks with a compact pseudocode trace; label the arrows as schematic rather than quantitative.

evidence.label: Figure 1. Program-of-layers (PoLAR) for two different inputs

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. Sequential MCTS (left) vs. End-to-end PoLAR network (right) for prediction of programs. (a) MCTS in the space of execution programs via sequential iterations of selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation. Each node represents a partial or complete execution program, and skip/repeat operations expand the search tree iteratively. This explicit and thorough search is expensive and impractical. (b) Our PoLAR trains an end-to-end, lightweight prediction network that directly produces a program representation composed of (i) a binary mask z^seg(x) segmenting layers into modules, and (ii) a vector of operation labels z^op(x) that applies one operation out of skip, keep, or repeat to each module. Our method is scalable in practice and does not require sequential search.

color.semantic_mapping: Four pastel stage boxes identify MCTS phases; red selected nodes and yellow stars identify the search trace; blue arrows and colored operation cells identify the direct predictor path.

encodings.x: MCTS stage order and input → network → execute → prediction direction
encodings.y: tree depth on the search side and mask/operation rows on the predictor side
encodings.color: MCTS stage, selected node, and skip/keep/repeat role
encodings.shape: circle/star tree nodes and segmented representation cells
encodings.line: solid and dashed arrows; red selected branch versus other branches
encodings.facet: MCTS sequential search versus PoLAR direct program output
encodings.text: stage names, π examples, z^seg/z^op labels, layer indices, and prediction

figures.data_and_statistics: Method-interface diagram, not a statistical display. The left panel is an illustrative search tree; the right panel gives an example binary segmentation mask and operation vector. No sample, unit, denominator, aggregation, repeated trial, or uncertainty is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Connects Figure 1’s program vocabulary to Section 2 offline MCTS and Section 3 learned predictor. It explains why Tables 2–10 compare PoLAR with sequential or local-routing baselines and why Figure 8 treats program candidates as the test-time search unit.
design_strengths: The four MCTS stages and the one-shot network are aligned on one input/output direction.
The two rows z^seg and z^op make the predictor interface concrete.
Caption states the practical cost distinction rather than leaving the comparison implicit.
design_weaknesses: Tree breadth and vector length are schematic and do not communicate the true search-space scale.
Stage colors and selected-node colors are not robust in grayscale.
The caption omits beam size and the maximum program-space dimensions.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair an iterative search-state panel with a direct-output schema panel; show the old computation path and its learned replacement using the same left-to-right semantics.

evidence.label: Figure 2. Sequential MCTS (left) vs. End-to-end PoLAR network (right)

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3. Accuracy of MCTS discovered programs under varying execution-depth budgets across five difficulty levels in DART-Math. We compare the original forward pass (orange) with 90–115% depth-budgeted programs (blue). Shaded regions denote the maximum gain achieved under the highest budget (115%).

color.semantic_mapping: Orange is the original path; a blue sequential gradient denotes 90, 95, 100, 105, 110, and 115% execution-depth budgets; light blue fill annotates the maximum 115% gain.

encodings.shape: circle markers for budgeted program points
encodings.text: model titles, gain@115% annotations, and shared legend

figures.data_and_statistics: Aggregated accuracy of MCTS-discovered programs at five DART-Math difficulty levels for four models, comparing the original full-depth path with total execution-depth budgets from 90% to 115%. The points have no displayed test-set denominator, repeated-run dispersion, failure count, or interval. The shaded region is a maximum-gain annotation, not statistical uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Primary visual evidence for the paper’s budget and recurrence mechanism. It supports Finding 1 and Table 1’s operator comparison, then supplies the depth context for Figure 4’s shorter valid programs and Figures 5–6’s scaling/depth–accuracy analyses.
design_strengths: A fixed 2×2 facet layout makes model trends comparable.
Shared x/y semantics and one baseline legend expose the budget sweep without separate captions.
Gain annotations direct attention to the highest-budget comparison.
design_weaknesses: Six blue budget traces are crowded in each small panel.
The shaded gain region resembles an uncertainty band even though it has a different meaning.
No sample size or dispersion is shown, so accuracy variation cannot be assessed.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a shared facet grid and one baseline plus ordered budget traces for a resource sweep; distinguish gain annotations from uncertainty through a separate visual treatment and explicit caption.

evidence.label: Figure 3. Accuracy of MCTS discovered programs under varying execution-depth budgets

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. Latent execution programs often admit shorter valid solutions. We compare the standard forward-pass depth with that of MCTS-discovered valid programs, for initially correct (C→C) and initially incorrect (W→C) inputs. Bars report total execution depth as a fraction of full model depth, with hatched overlays indicating effective depth (the number of unique layers).

color.semantic_mapping: Four model colors identify columns; light versions and diagonal hatch overlays identify non-recurrent/effective depth relative to solid total depth; C→C and W→C are row conditions.

encodings.x: difficulty level 1–5 within each model/condition panel
encodings.text: model titles, C→C/W→C row labels, and shared legend

figures.data_and_statistics: Bars summarize total layer executions and unique executed layers for MCTS-discovered valid programs, expressed as a fraction of full model depth. C→C conditions on initially correct standard inference; W→C conditions on initially incorrect answers corrected by a valid program. No uncertainty or sample counts are displayed.
figures.evidence_relation: Visualizes Finding 2’s claim that many valid programs are shorter. The total/effective decomposition relates Figure 3’s execution budget to Figure 8’s unique-depth CDF and Table 4’s latency cost.
design_strengths: Solid and hatched overlays separate total computation from unique-layer structure in the same mark.
Common scales across eight facets support model and correctness-condition comparisons.
Caption defines the C→C/W→C conditioning and hatch semantics.
design_weaknesses: Narrow bars and a 80–100% y-range make small differences hard to read.
No sample sizes or variability accompany the conditional fractions.
The model color palette remains partly dependent on color despite hatch redundancy.
figures.reusable_pattern: Overlay effective components with hatching on total bars, while preserving a common baseline and row-condition split for resource decompositions.

evidence.label: Figure 4. Latent execution programs often admit shorter valid solutions

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5. (a) Test-time scaling via recurrence over layer segments. Allowing more latent execution steps through segment recurrence leads to a monotonic increase in the probability of discovering valid execution programs across models. (b) Recurrence and skipping are increasingly demanded for harder inputs. The fraction of inputs relying on layer recurrence or skipping to be solved increases with increasing difficulty for most models, except LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, whose deviation is explained by effective difficulty in Table 1.

color.semantic_mapping: Model colors are reused across panel (a) and the four model facets; solid lines mean require recurrence and dashed lines mean require skip.

encodings.x: additional recurrence steps in (a) and difficulty 1–5 in (b)
encodings.y: valid-program probability in (a), or fraction requiring an operator in (b)
encodings.facet: budget curve plus four model-specific demand facets
encodings.text: operator line-style key, model legend, axis titles, and panel labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel (a) aggregates the probability of finding a valid program within an additional-recurrence budget; panel (b) aggregates the fraction of solvable inputs whose program relies on recurrence or skipping by difficulty. Neither panel displays denominators, repeated-run dispersion, failure counts, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Operationalizes Finding 3: larger latent budgets expand the feasible program space, while harder inputs demand non-trivial operators. It interprets patterns in Table 1 and prepares the depth–accuracy relation of Figure 6.
design_strengths: The resource curve and difficulty-conditioned operator demand are separated into labeled panels.
Model color and line style jointly encode two dimensions of the mechanism.
The caption records the exceptional LLaMA trend and points back to Table 1.
design_weaknesses: Four narrow facets plus two legends compress labels and tick marks.
The caption leaves the model-color map and exact fractions to the visual legend.
No denominator or uncertainty is shown for any fraction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Combine a resource-scaling panel with small multiples for condition prevalence, using line style for operator and color/facet for model; state the fraction denominator explicitly in reuse.

evidence.label: Figure 5. Test-time scaling via recurrence over layer segments

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6. Accuracy vs. total layer executions. For each model, we report how the average accuracy of valid execution programs changes with the total number of layer executions (% of base model depth). Across models and difficulty levels, accuracy increases with executed layers, revealing a consistent effect of depth-scaling.

color.semantic_mapping: Difficulty levels 1–5 are encoded by point color; model identity is encoded by the four facet titles.

encodings.x: total layer executions as % of original depth
encodings.y: average accuracy of valid execution programs

figures.data_and_statistics: Each point represents an aggregated average accuracy at a total execution-depth percentage for one model and difficulty level. The chart reports a relationship rather than a fitted effect; no error bars, sample weights, denominator, or repeated-run uncertainty is displayed.
figures.evidence_relation: Provides Finding 3(c)’s mechanism evidence that deeper/recurrent execution generally raises accuracy, complementing Figure 5’s budget view and explaining why Figure 8 can improve performance without always using full unique depth.
design_strengths: Common axes across four model facets make the monotonic trend visually comparable.
Color is reserved for difficulty while model identity is direct-labeled.
Point placement shows the compute–accuracy tradeoff without adding a potentially misleading fit line.
design_weaknesses: Point overlap at high depth hides multiplicity and sample density.
No trend line, uncertainty, or point-count cue is provided.
Difficulty colors are hard to distinguish in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Facet by entity, color by condition, and plot a continuous compute proxy against outcome; add transparent point density or sample counts when overlap matters.

evidence.label: Figure 6. Accuracy vs. total layer executions

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7. Structural bias of valid execution programs. Valid programs rely primarily on contiguous layer segments as modules (a) and require at most one recurrence of each module (b).

color.semantic_mapping: Blue intensity encodes segment-structure percentages in the heatmap; orange bars encode the fraction by maximum recurrence count; cell labels provide numeric redundancy.

encodings.x: segment length in (a) and maximum recurrence count per segment in (b)
encodings.y: number of consecutive layers within a segment in (a), or fraction in (b)
encodings.color: heatmap intensity versus orange recurrence-count bars
encodings.facet: structural composition matrix versus recurrence-count marginal summary
encodings.text: percentage labels in cells, categorical axis titles, and panel labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel (a) reports the percentage of valid-program segments by segment length and consecutive-layer count; panel (b) reports the fraction by maximum recurrence count per segment. Values are point percentages with no sample total, repeated-run uncertainty, or confidence interval.
figures.evidence_relation: Directly supports Finding 4 and the segment-level representation in Section 3: contiguous short modules and at most one recurrence motivate the K_max bound and z^seg/z^op design shown in Figure 2.
design_strengths: The heatmap and marginal bar answer complementary structural questions in one compact object.
Cell percentages preserve numeric readability even when color differences are subtle.
The categorical layout makes the “at most one recurrence” pattern easy to inspect.
design_weaknesses: Blank or zero cells in the triangular matrix are not defined in the caption.
The bar chart does not expose the denominator or an explicit sum check.
Heatmap intensity is not robust to grayscale reproduction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a discrete structural heatmap with a one-dimensional marginal distribution; annotate cells directly and define empty/zero cells and denominators.

evidence.label: Figure 7. Structural bias of valid execution programs

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8. Pass@k accuracy and unique depth on LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, averaged across DART-Math DM-1 to DM-5. (a) reports macro-averaged pass@k accuracy for Base (sampling) and PoLAR. (b) reports the CDF of the shortest successful execution program among the top-5 candidates, measured by unique executed layers as a percentage of the original model depth.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue denotes Base (sampling) and orange denotes PoLAR; in panel (b), Base is a dashed full-depth reference and PoLAR is an orange step CDF.

encodings.x: k=1–5 in (a), or unique depth as % of original depth in (b)
encodings.y: macro-averaged pass@k in (a), or CDF in (b)
encodings.shape: bars in (a) and an ECDF step in (b)
encodings.line: dashed Base full-depth reference versus solid PoLAR CDF
encodings.facet: performance panel paired with unique-depth cost panel
encodings.text: panel labels, shared legend, and 100% reference line

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel (a) macro-averages pass@k accuracy across DART-Math DM-1–DM-5 for LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct. Panel (b) is the CDF of the shortest successful program among the top five candidates, measured by unique executed layers relative to original depth. No error bars, sample count, or uncertainty band is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Combines Table 2’s main pass@k comparison with the cost/structure evidence in Figures 4 and 6. It is the compact endpoint of the narrative: program-level exploration improves accuracy while successful candidates can use fewer unique layers.
design_strengths: Accuracy and computation cost are shown together under the same Base/PoLAR semantic.
The CDF directly exposes the distribution of shorter successful programs rather than only a mean.
Caption defines macro averaging, top-five candidates, and unique depth.
design_weaknesses: The fixed 100% Base line and PoLAR step can visually overlap near the right boundary.
CDF sample size is not stated, and the narrow pass@k y-range limits precise reading.
Color remains necessary for the bar-panel identity despite the line-style redundancy in panel (b).
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair performance-at-k bars with a cost distribution CDF so a single figure answers whether a method is more accurate and how much computation successful candidates use.

evidence.label: Figure 8. Pass@k accuracy and unique depth

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1. Accuracy (%) of programs searched for DART-Math (Diff 1–5) in different spaces: Base (standard forward), Skip (layer skipping), Loop (layer recurrence), and Skip&Loop (skipping + recurrence). Gain reports the absolute gain of Skip&Loop over Base. Bold indicates the best result, and underline indicates the second-best result in each row.

tables.uncertainty: Point accuracy percentages only; no uncertainty, repeated-run variation, or failure count.
tables.data_and_statistics: DART-Math DM-1–DM-5 values for four models and four execution spaces. Gain is the absolute Skip&Loop minus Base percentage-point difference, not a mean or interval.
tables.evidence_relation: Primary evidence for Finding 1. Figure 3 shows budget behavior, Figures 5–7 explain recurrence and structure, and Appendix Tables 5–7 expand the learned predictor comparison.
design_strengths: Four model groups and five difficulty rows align all operator spaces in one decision surface.
Bold, underline, and blue Gain provide three scan paths for best, second-best, and improvement.
design_weaknesses: Twenty rows are dense in a single column.
Blue Gain and underline contrast are weaker in grayscale, and no per-row test denominator is supplied.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use model-group bands, fixed operator columns, and an explicit gain column to compare compositional inference operators.

caption.text: Table 4. Component-wise inference overhead and end-to-end latency of PoLAR on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat with 24 layers. The additional components introduce negligible overhead compared with a standard forward pass, while PoLAR reduces end-to-end latency and improves accuracy.

tables.data_and_statistics: Two blocks report component latency/equivalent layers/% full forward and Base versus PoLAR end-to-end average layers/latency/relative runtime/accuracy gain.
tables.evidence_relation: Closes the cost loop from Figures 4 and 8 to the Section 4.2 runtime claim; Appendix Table 11 supplies predictor parameter-size context.

tables.reusable_pattern: Use two labeled blocks to separate added component cost from end-to-end benefit, keeping a common equivalent-compute bridge.

tables.uncertainty: Parameter counts and normalized ratios are point values; no counting method, uncertainty, or repeated measurement is reported.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four rows give base LLM parameter size, learned predictor parameter size, and predictor/base percentage.
tables.evidence_relation: Complements Table 4’s inference overhead with Appendix D.3’s size claim and serves as a reproducibility-oriented accounting table.
design_strengths: Base, predictor, and normalized ratio are aligned in one compact table.
Units B/M and ratio percentage make the scale comparison immediately checkable.
design_weaknesses: No parameter-counting procedure or trainable/frozen split is stated in the table.
Four-decimal ratio precision suggests more certainty than the surrounding approximate size claim.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report original component size, added component size, and normalized ratio together when documenting lightweight add-ons.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 defines program-of-layers semantics; Figure 2 contrasts offline sequential search with direct prediction; Figures 3–7 establish budget, shorter-path, operator-demand, depth–accuracy, and structural-bias mechanisms; Figure 8 and Tables 2–4 close the accuracy/OOD/latency case; Tables 5–11 provide backbone slices and parameter accounting.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Figure captions generally use a bold title followed by setup, encoding, comparison, and often a finding; Table 2/3/5–10 captions are shorter and defer metric definitions to prose, whereas Table 4 states its main cost conclusion. Figure 3 names the shading as maximum gain but not as non-uncertainty, leaving a possible band ambiguity.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Pass@k tables use Method × p@ × DM-1–DM-5; OOD tables use Method × ASDiv × MAWPS × a spanned MMLU-Pro subject header; Table 4 uses two named blocks; Table 11 uses base/predictor/ratio columns. This supports cross-backbone replication but makes wide OOD headers dense.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: The z^seg/z^op interface in Figure 2 is motivated by Figures 3–7 and tested by Table 1 operator comparisons, Tables 2–3 main/OOD results, Figure 8 pass@k/depth, and Table 4 runtime. Tables 5–10 expand the same result schemas by backbone. The PDF has no independent theorem/proof visual object; Table 1 is the explicit execution-space operator ablation, while Figures 3–7 provide empirical mechanism evidence.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Table 2 is expanded by Tables 5–7, Table 3 by Tables 8–10, and Table 4’s lightweight predictor claim by Table 11. Appendix D also defines the dataset split and training configuration but contains no additional Figure.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: PDF body/table typography is consistently Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern, while figure-internal plots use Arial/Calibri-like sans-serif and imported diagrams use additional asset fonts. Caption labels and bold titles provide the most stable cross-object hierarchy.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Orange often means baseline/original and blue often means Base/budget, but Figures 5–6 repurpose color for model or difficulty. Figure 4 reuses model colors and hatching; table Gain and PoLAR row highlights form separate local color systems. There is no fully global semantic palette.

most_reusable_patterns: Freeze a shared function library and draw two input-specific execution paths with operation labels and pseudocode, as in Figures 1–2.
Use fixed facets and shared scales to place budget, difficulty, depth, and accuracy in a mechanism sequence, as in Figures 3, 5, and 6.
Combine solid bars with hatch overlays or performance bars with a cost CDF to put accuracy and computation on the same decision surface.
Use explicit Gain/Δ columns, hierarchical benchmark headers, and isomorphic appendix tables to make operator, pass@k, OOD, and latency claims auditable.
failure_patterns: Figures and tables provide no sample counts, repeated-run dispersion, or uncertainty encoding.
Figure 3 gain shading can be mistaken for an uncertainty band.
Several plots rely heavily on color, while Figure 5 facets and wide OOD tables become small or dense at page scale.
The public repository exposes only a matching Figure 1 PNG and no editable source for Figures 2–8 or Tables 1–11.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper moves from program-language diagrams through MCTS structural evidence to a PoLAR accuracy/cost closure and isomorphic appendix slices, binding dynamic-depth mechanism, performance, and efficiency while leaving statistical denominators, uncertainty, and editable visual sources underspecified.
